text:
The Long Way Home: Apollo 13

On the afternoon of April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rocket lifted from its pad in Florida carrying three men toward the Moon. Jim Lovell, the commander, was a veteran of three earlier flights and was making his fourth trip into space. Fred Haise, the lunar module pilot, was a newcomer. The third seat belonged to Jack Swigert, who had joined the crew only days before. The original command module pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been exposed to German measles and was grounded by flight surgeons, so Swigert took his place. The launch was almost flawless, and the mission, the third planned landing on the Moon, seemed likely to be another success in a program that had already begun to feel routine. Television networks had stopped broadcasting the crew's transmissions live.

The spacecraft was a stack of three parts. The command module, which the crew named Odyssey, was the cone where the men would live and where they would return to Earth. Behind it sat the service module, a cylinder holding the main engine, the fuel cells that made electricity, and the tanks of oxygen and hydrogen that fed them. Attached to the front was the lunar module, named Aquarius, a spindly landing craft meant to carry two men down to a highland region called Fra Mauro.

For two days the flight went smoothly. Then, on the evening of April 13, about fifty-five hours into the mission and nearly two hundred thousand miles from home, Mission Control in Houston asked the crew to stir the supercold tanks in the service module. Stirring kept the contents from settling and gave more accurate readings of how much remained. It was a routine chore. Swigert flipped the switch.

Moments later the crew heard a loud bang and felt the ship shudder. Warning lights lit up across the panel. Lovell spoke the words that became famous, though in slightly altered form: "Houston, we've had a problem." Voltage on the electrical systems was dropping. Out of the window, Lovell saw gas streaming into space. Oxygen was leaving the service module, and it was leaving fast.

The cause was later traced to a chain of small errors beginning years earlier. One of the oxygen tanks had been dropped slightly during handling on the ground, damaging its internal plumbing. During a pre-launch test, technicians had struggled to drain it and had run heaters for hours, which fused the protective coating on the wiring inside. When Swigert stirred the tank in flight, a spark ignited that wiring, the pressure surged, and the tank burst. The blast tore away a panel on the side of the service module and crippled the second oxygen tank as well.

Without oxygen the fuel cells died, and without the fuel cells the command module had no power, no water, and no way to breathe. Odyssey carried batteries, but they were needed for the final descent through Earth's atmosphere and could not last the four days of the trip home. In Houston, flight director Gene Kranz gathered his team and set the priority plainly: the goal was no longer the Moon but bringing the men back alive.

The answer lay in the lunar module. Aquarius had been designed to support two men for roughly two days on the Moon's surface, and it had its own oxygen, water, power, and engine. Lovell, Haise, and Swigert crowded into it and used it as a lifeboat, shutting down Odyssey almost completely to conserve what little energy was left. The plan required stretching a craft built for two men and two days to keep three men alive for nearly four.

The trajectory presented another problem. The ship was on a path that would swing around the Moon and return to Earth, but the course had been adjusted so that it would miss Earth by a wide margin if nothing was done. About five hours after the accident, the crew fired the lunar module's descent engine to put the ship back on a path toward home. After looping around the far side of the Moon, where they passed farther from Earth than any humans before or since, they fired the engine again to speed the return. Few people on the ground or in the ship slept much.

Then the conditions inside the ship grew harsh. With almost every system off, the temperature fell to just above freezing, and moisture condensed on the walls. The crew rationed water severely to keep the lunar module's electronics cool, and Haise developed a fever from an infection. Swigert and Lovell wore their moon boots to keep their feet warm. They were exhausted, dehydrated, and cold.

A more urgent danger crept in quietly. Carbon dioxide, which the men exhaled, was building up in the cabin. Canisters of lithium hydroxide absorbed it, but the lunar module had only enough for two men for two days. The command module held plenty of spare canisters, but they were square, and the receptacles in the lunar module were round. Engineers on the ground gathered the same materials the crew had aboard, including cardboard from flight manuals, plastic bags, hoses from spacesuits, and duct tape, and devised a makeshift adapter. They read the instructions to the crew over the radio, and the men built it. Within hours the carbon dioxide readings fell back to safe levels.

Navigation was the next challenge. With the guidance systems shut down to save power, the crew needed another way to line up the ship for a critical engine burn. Lovell used the Earth itself as a reference, holding the line of sunrise across its curved surface in a window while the burn was carried out by hand. It worked. The ship was on a correct course for the narrow corridor through which it had to enter the atmosphere, a gap only a few degrees wide.

Meanwhile, back in Houston and at a simulator in Florida, engineers, including Mattingly, worked out a procedure to bring Odyssey back to life. They needed to restart the command module with only the power in its entry batteries, and they had to do it in the right order so that nothing would fail. The checklist was written in a matter of days, which would normally have taken months.

On the final day, the crew separated the service module, and for the first time they saw the damage. An entire panel was gone, and the side of the ship was scorched and ragged. Lovell reported it to the ground, and everyone realized how close the disaster had been. Then the crew moved back into Odyssey, powered it up, and released the lunar module, which had saved them, to burn up in the atmosphere.

Reentry brought a final tense wait. The ship's plasma sheath normally blocks radio for about three minutes, and controllers watched the clock. Three minutes passed with no word. Then four. The silence stretched, and the room in Houston stopped breathing. At last Swigert's voice came through, and the crowd erupted. Parachutes opened, and the capsule dropped into the South Pacific near Samoa on April 17, almost six days after launch. A recovery ship picked up the men, tired, thin, and well.

Apollo 13 never reached the Moon, yet it is often counted among the finest hours of the space program. Investigators redesigned the oxygen tanks, and the program carried on with later landings. But what people remember is the way a failing ship was saved by improvisation, close teamwork between the crew and the ground, and a refusal to give up.
